reason: The passage demonstrates the opposite of the statement. When Joab offers criticism regarding David's plan to count the people, David explicitly rejects it. The text states 'דְבַר־הַמֶּלֶךְ חָזַק עַל־יוֹאָב' ('the king's word was firm against Joab'), showing David doubling down on his decision despite Joab's objections. This arrogant refusal to accept criticism directly leads to catastrophic consequences—God sends a plague killing seventy thousand people. Only after experiencing divine judgment does David show humility and repentance ('חָטָאתִי מְאֹד' - 'I have sinned greatly'). The narrative structure teaches that rejecting criticism arrogantly leads to disaster, and while David's eventual repentance is virtuous, the text does not model 'humility in the face of criticism' as good leadership. Rather, it warns against precisely what David initially did—ignoring wise counsel.
